item.title: What “Stay-At-Home Sons” Get Right, and What They Get Wrong
item.description:
Social Life

What “Stay-At-Home Sons” Get Right, and What They Get Wrong

Why adulthood may need a new definition

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Living at home doesn’t automatically signal immaturity or failure.
  • Economic realities are reshaping traditional milestones of adulthood.
  • Independence looks different across families and cultures.
  • Healthy adulthood is defined by responsibility, not where you live.
Source: Askar Abayev / Pexels

If you’ve spent any time on social media recently, you’ve probably heard the term “stay-at-home sons” used as a joke or an insult, or maybe almost as a badge of honor.

This trend is about adult men who still live with their parents, often while working, going to school, or figuring out their next step. Some who see the trend may laugh at it, thinking it to be ridiculous, but what this trend is really poking at is the idea that adulthood doesn’t mean what it used to mean. It simply looks different now.

For generations, moving out was viewed as one of the clearest markers of adulthood. Now, people are questioning that idea.

The meaning of independence is changing

Developmental psychologists have long described the years between the late teens and early 30s as emerging adulthood, which is defined by the gradual process of building an independent adult life. Living with parents doesn’t automatically interrupt that process.

According to the Pew Research Center, 18 percent of adults ages 25-34 were living with their parents in 2023, with men slightly more likely than women to do so. The majority of respondents stated that living at home has had a positive effect on their finances, and nearly three-quarters contribute financially to the household in one way or another, but this isn’t what people generally think of when they think of a grown man living at home.

The assumption has always been that living at home reflects laziness, immaturity, or a failure to launch. However, with today’s economy, some people may have difficulties living on their own. Living independently can cause some adults to avoid responsibility just as easily as it could be for someone else living at home to embrace it.

When family support becomes dependency

When we think about what it means to be independent, we have legitimate conversations about what a person contributes versus their age and their living situation. Living independently requires being more present and involved with making household contributions while working toward financial security alongside emotional maturity.

Not every situation is healthy. There is an important psychological difference between those who are receiving support and those who are avoiding adulthood.

While support creates stability as someone builds the next stage of life, dependency removes chances to build confidence to figure things out on your own. The goal in life is always to grow and learn and become at peace with who you are.

article continues after advertisement

Staying at home may have started as a reasonable financial decision, but it becomes a problem when it turns into parents still doing the laundry or taking the car to the mechanic, while the adult child refuses to contribute anything to the household. That form of dependency can continue to lead into retroactive childlike behavior, and that’s where the real issue is.

Looking beyond the label

Social media often rewards simple labels. “Stay-at-home son” is catchy because it offers an immediate judgment. And what’s interesting about that is that it allows people to make their own assumptions around what that label means.

But real life is a lot more nuanced. What’s now considered a predictable life path may not appear or manifest the way it did 50 years ago, or even just 10 years ago. The world has changed, and so will expectations. The better question to ask isn’t whether someone still lives with their parents, but whether they’re taking responsibility for their life.

Adulthood isn’t defined by where you sleep at night. It’s defined by how you take responsibility for the life you’re building.

item.title: Responding to Change at Work
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Responding to Change at Work

Choosing healthy ways to meet your needs while on the job

Posted August 24, 2026

Key points
  • Change seems inevitable at work. How do you respond?
  • It's important to consider how the Big 4 universal human needs come into play during times of change.
  • Frequently, people meet their needs in unhealthy or unproductive ways when facing change at work.
  • Consider choosing healthier, more productive approaches to change like the ones described in this article.

We’re frequently expected to adapt to changes at work. These could be changes in policy, work group configuration, the organizational hierarchy, or job duties. Underlying our responses to change is the issue of how we will get our innate needs met in light of the changes in our work world.

In a previous post, I explained the “Big 4” universal human needs or motivations as they related to job satisfaction. These Big 4 are 1) contribution or calling, 2) choice or control, 3) competence or capability, and 4) connection or community. Meeting these four needs is what we humans require to feel like we’re living our best life. When we have change thrust upon us at work, the ways we get these needs met at work may be threatened, and it can be tempting to resort to unhealthy or unproductive methods to meet them.

Let’s start with contribution or calling

We humans have a need to feel like what we do with our time and effort is meaningful and purposeful. With changes to your work, it can feel like those who lead the organization are implying that what you used to do before wasn’t worthwhile, and hence the need to change what you’re doing. That can feel defeating. Or perhaps some or all aspects of the change seem meaningless, and therefore not very motivating.

In response, it can be tempting to disengage and simply go through the motions. Doing so isn’t healthy for you or the organization. So what can you do instead?

It may fall to you to create meaning in your work. Frequently, leaders fail to illuminate how each person’s job responsibilities contribute to the mission of the organization. So you may have to uncover and remind yourself of how your work makes some sort of difference as a necessary piece of fulfilling the organization’s mission. You might also choose to look for ways to alter your work to make it more meaningful, even if that means doing a bit more than is expected or that falls under what you’re being paid to do. Rather than seeing it as providing uncompensated work, recognize the personal benefits that come from doing something meaningful.

Choice and control

When it comes to meeting the need for choice and control, an unhealthy approach is to rebel against the changes. When we are told we have to do something, it’s natural to resist, even if just psychologically. A healthier or more productive way to respond to the threat to your autonomy is to focus on what you have control over. For example, you may not have much choice in what you are responsible for getting done, but there may be latitude in your choice of how to accomplish what you need to. In a previous post, I wrote about this process, which psychologists call job crafting.

Competence or capability

When it comes to competence or capability, change can threaten your established ways of being successful. Change at work frequently requires you to learn new things, do new things, or at least use skills that may be rusty. An unhealthy or unproductive response is to continually question the reasons or legitimacy for change. Doing so can seemingly provide an excuse to drag your feet.

article continues after advertisement

A healthier or more productive way to address the need for competence and capability is to focus on the end result. The experience of the change can be stressful and unsettling, but what knowledge, skills, or abilities will you gain as a result? How might these aspects of growth possibly contribute to your future success or professional advancement?

Last, consider the need for connection and community

Frequently, change at work results in people meeting this need through bonding over shared gossip, complaining, or second-guessing leadership. It makes sense that people all going through the same stressful experience would look to each other for support. However, as I wrote about in previous posts, there are recognized problems created by gossip and cliques.

So, rather than meeting the need for connection and community through commiseration, and possibly excluding others who don’t share similar views, is there a way to support each other more productively? For example, might the team agree to focus on positive ways to help each other cope, such as offering help to those who could use some, and reinforcing progress and small wins along the way?

Even when change is positive and desired, it inherently involves some degree of stress. During times of change, I reflect on the importance of considering the Big 4 universal human needs. To the extent that meeting those needs is threatened, people may find themselves resisting the change, or meeting these needs in ways that are less healthy and productive than had previously been the case. Whether you’re a leader or working in the trenches, I encourage you to give the Big 4 some thought as well.
